problem: Drops 'after the level in the blood peaks'. 'Half of it to leave the blood' can be read as timed from taking the dose, but the half-life runs from the peak, and the blood level is still rising for hours after snorting or smoking.
claim_says: after the level in the blood peaks, it takes about 10 to 12 hours
suggested_fix: After the blood level peaks, it takes about 10 to 12 hours to fall by half.

problem: The heading asks how long the effects last. The claim gives only when effects and blood levels peak, so the short line cannot answer it, and readers may take the But's 'keeps rising for hours' as how long the effects last (the half-life claim warns these differ).
claim_says: heart rate and blood pressure peaked within about 15 minutes in both studies
suggested_fix: How fast do the effects of a snorted dose peak?

problem: 'Only one lab has studied this' follows the blood-level sentence, so it reads as if only one lab measured the blood level. The claim cites an independent lab for the blood peak (2.66 hours on average); it is the two effect-timing studies that share one lab.
claim_says: in an independent laboratory, where plasma was sampled to 72 hours
suggested_fix: The amount in the blood keeps rising for hours. The timing of the effects comes from one lab.

problem: The timing of the high was reported in only one of the two studies; the point presents it as a result of both.
claim_says: subjective ratings at 15 minutes in the one study that reported their timing
suggested_fix: Heart rate and blood pressure peaked within about 15 minutes; so did the high, in the one study that timed it.

problem: 'by route' is a technical word for the target reader.
claim_says: Most of a snorted dose reaches the bloodstream
suggested_fix: How much of a dose reaches the blood when it is snorted or smoked?

problem: The But covers only the smoking figures. The short line's first sentence ('Most of a snorted dose') rests on one study of 8 men, which the But does not say.
claim_says: Absolute bioavailability after a single intranasal dose was 79.4% (SD 13.1) in 8 men
suggested_fix: The snorting figure comes from one study of 8 men. For smoking, studies measure it in different ways.

problem: The first sentence restates the heading's premise ('the two mirror-image forms of meth') instead of answering.
claim_says: the two methamphetamine enantiomers differed in disposition and in effect
suggested_fix: Yes. In one study, the 'l' form felt weaker and wore off sooner.

problem: Drops the route. The claim is restricted to single snorted (intranasal) doses; the But restores the lab setting and the population but not the route. Low priority, but this is a key-facts card.
claim_says: single intranasal doses raised heart rate, blood pressure and positive subjective ratings
suggested_fix: One snorted dose raises heart rate and blood pressure and makes people feel high.

problem: Has no 'in lab' or 'snorted', and a careful reader could object that it depends on the dose: in one of the two studies only the larger dose raised heart rate and blood pressure.
claim_says: at all three doses vs placebo in one study and at the larger dose
suggested_fix: In lab studies, one snorted dose of meth raised heart rate and blood pressure. (answer stays true)

problem: 'did not make attention or memory worse' turns 'no measurable worsening in small studies' into 'no worsening'. The claim says small or moderate impairments cannot be excluded (the quiz answer already says 'not measurably').
claim_says: The studies were too small to exclude small or moderate impairments
suggested_fix: In lab tests, single doses did not measurably worsen attention or memory.

problem: Does not say that small or moderate harm cannot be ruled out, the main limit of a 'no worse' finding. Also 'from one research group' is not true of all the studies: the two main studies and the review came from one group, but 9 of the 16 reviewed studies came from other labs and are seen only through that review.
claim_says: The studies were too small to exclude small or moderate impairments
suggested_fix: The studies were small, so small or moderate harm can't be ruled out. Binges were not tested.

problem: Not all the studies came from one research group: 7 of the 16 reviewed studies did; the rest came from other labs, known here only through that group's review.
claim_says: the studies from other laboratories are known here only from that review
suggested_fix: The studies were small. The two main ones, and the review of the others, came from one research group.

problem: Same as the short line: 'did not make memory worse' is stronger than the claim's 'did not measurably worsen'. Since small or moderate harm was not excluded, a careful reader could dispute 'true'.
claim_says: did not measurably worsen attention, memory or reaction-time tasks
suggested_fix: In lab tests, single doses of meth did not measurably worsen memory. (true)

problem: The heading asks 'why', but the claim says the reason has not been tested (tolerance within a dose, or effects that follow the rate of rise). The short line only restates the heading's premise and gives no answer.
claim_says: Whether this reflects tolerance developing within a single dose
suggested_fix: Do the effects fade while the drug is still in the blood?

problem: In the main study the felt effects peaked at about 17 to 18 minutes (heart rate at about 12), so 'within about 15 minutes' is a little short; the statement says 12 to 18 minutes. Minor (the plain says 'a quarter of an hour'). The same applies to how[0].
claim_says: Peak subjective effect at about 18 min (SE 2.1)
suggested_fix: The felt effects peak within about 18 minutes and fade while blood levels stay high.

problem: The figures are 43% (smaller dose) and 37% (larger dose). 'A third to a half' stretches the upper end to 50%; 'about two fifths' fits both. Minor; the plain uses the same wide range. The same applies to how[1].
claim_says: About −43% of total daily calories at 5 mg and −37% at 10 mg
suggested_fix: One dose cut how much people ate that day by about two fifths.

problem: The heading asks about meth, but the only figures are for stimulants grouped (US survey: stimulants other than cocaine, 1990 to 1992).
claim_says: Both surveys lump stimulants together, and neither gives a number for meth alone.
suggested_fix: How many people who use stimulants like meth become dependent?

problem: The claim's biggest limit (rated down two levels for it) is that neither survey gives a figure for meth alone, and the But does not say so while the heading asks about meth. Also, 'milder diagnoses' is not the claim's wording (it says a broader outcome, abuse or dependence).
claim_says: neither gives a figure for methamphetamine alone
suggested_fix: Neither survey gives a number for meth alone. This one also counted people who had only just started.

problem: The picture has no note. The 11 in 100 is for stimulants other than cocaine grouped, from a 1990 to 1992 US survey, and the tobacco comparison was measured differently (separate survey, daily smokers only).
claim_says: tobacco use came from a separate 1991 survey and dependence was assessed for daily smoking
suggested_fix: Add note: "US survey, 1990 to 1992: stimulants other than cocaine, not meth alone. Tobacco was measured differently."

problem: The survey did not ask people 'were you ever dependent?'. It used a structured interview to check diagnostic criteria, so the point misdescribes how the figure was found.
claim_says: had ever met DSM-III-R criteria for dependence
suggested_fix: In the early 1990s, a US survey used set interview questions to find who had ever been dependent on a drug they had used.

problem: 'a milder diagnosis' is not in the claim, which calls abuse 'a related diagnosis' and the Australian outcome 'broader'.
claim_says: dependence or a related diagnosis called abuse
suggested_fix: An Australian survey asked in a different way. It estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years, also counting a related diagnosis called 'abuse'.

problem: 'instead of meth': the 41% and 17% drug choices pool meth with d-amphetamine. The plain says 'a stimulant dose'.
claim_says: Drug portions (methamphetamine and d-amphetamine pooled) were chosen on 41% of opportunities
suggested_fix: In lab choice tests, people often chose small amounts of cash over a stimulant dose.

problem: 'the difference' is not explained. The short line never mentions the two cash amounts, so the reader cannot tell what difference money might have made.
claim_says: so the difference may reflect the people as much as the money
suggested_fix: Only 13 men, in one lab. Different men got different cash amounts, so it can't show what more cash does.

problem: 'most symptoms eased' holds only for what people reported themselves. On the staff-rated checklist only 8 of 30 items changed, and its craving and low-mood items did not (how[1] already says 'they reported').
claim_says: on the rater-scored checklist only 8 of 30 items changed significantly
suggested_fix: After stopping, most symptoms people reported eased within one to two weeks. Low mood and craving lasted longer.

problem: Drops the claim's scope 'in humans, as people use it' (its GRADE note says the animal evidence uses regimens unlike human use), so 'Nobody has shown either way' reads as covering all research. It also repeats the heading's question; on the key-facts card the question sits right above it.
claim_says: as people use it, causes lasting loss of or damage to dopamine neurons in humans
suggested_fix: Not shown either way in people, as they actually use meth.

problem: Gives the two small follow-ups where the protein rose but drops the counterweight the claim pairs with them: studies comparing groups found no link with time since last use.
claim_says: while cross-sectional studies found no relation with time since last use
suggested_fix: In two small studies the protein rose again after people stopped; other studies found no link with time off meth.

problem: The 3 vs 1 in 1,000 figure is from one of the two studies, over about 7 years, in people with meth- or amphetamine-related diagnoses. The point attributes it to both studies, drops the time frame and drops the claim's caveat that misclassified diagnoses are a plausible explanation.
claim_says: in one, 0.30% vs 0.11% over about 7 years
suggested_fix: On the other side, two health-record studies found Parkinson's more often in people with meth diagnoses (in one, about 3 vs 1 in 1,000 over 7 years). Some may be other conditions.

problem: 'Does heavy use change...' asks about cause. The claim compares groups and cannot show that use changed anything (the difference may predate use); paired with the short line it invites a 'yes'.
claim_says: These designs cannot show whether the difference reflects lost nerve terminals
suggested_fix: Is the dopamine system different in people who used meth heavily?

problem: No comparison group. 'After heavy use, brain scans show less' reads as a fall caused by use (before against after), but the claim compares people who used heavily with people who do not use.
claim_says: lower on average than in people who do not use
suggested_fix: People who used meth heavily have less of one dopamine protein on scans than people who don't, on average.

problem: Gives only two explanations (damage, or there before use) and drops the third the claim names: the brain making less of the protein. With only two options, any drug effect looks like damage.
claim_says: lost nerve terminals, reduced transporter expression or differences that predate use
suggested_fix: Scans cannot tell if this is damage, the brain making less of the protein, or a difference from before use.

problem: Same as the But: drops the third explanation, the brain making less of the protein.
claim_says: damaged nerve endings, the brain making less of the protein, or a difference
suggested_fix: Scans can't tell if this means damage, the brain making less of the protein, or a difference that was there before.

problem: 'Other studies found no such link' is wider than the claim. Four small cross-sectional studies found no link with time off meth, but another small follow-up reported a 20% rise over 2 weeks (first scan taken while urine was still positive).
claim_says: reported a mean 20% rise over 2 weeks
suggested_fix: Only five people, with nobody who doesn't use scanned twice. Four other small studies found no link with time off meth.

problem: The statement counts four cross-sectional analyses since v0.5.0 added Sekine et al. (2001); the point says three. The claim's own plain text (and its GRADE note) still say three and should be aligned too.
claim_says: Four cross-sectional analyses, including this programme's own baseline study, found no relation
suggested_fix: Four small studies found no link between time off meth and the protein level.

problem: 'not damage' is not in the claim. The authors contrast low stored dopamine with more of the protein, not with damage, and the study could not test it. The main limit, that only one lab has reported the raised signal, is also missing.
claim_says: reflects low stored dopamine rather than more of the protein
suggested_fix: Researchers think this shows low stored dopamine, which the study could not test. One lab only, and the studies are small.

problem: 'had stopped for over 3 years': the claim gives a mean of 3.4 years with a minimum of 3 months, so not everyone had stopped that long.
claim_says: abstinent a mean of 3.4 years (minimum 3 months) found binding about 10% lower
suggested_fix: In one study of people who had stopped for about 3 years on average, it was about 10% lower.

problem: 'some changes may not last' presumes the differences are changes caused by meth; the claim says 'differences'.
claim_says: so some differences may be temporary
suggested_fix: Smoking, schooling and low mood also differ, and some differences may not last.

problem: Drops 'in several regions' (so it reads as total grey matter) and the claim's caveat that the growth passed only a lenient statistical test.
claim_says: grey matter increased in several regions over the following month (at an uncorrected statistical threshold)
suggested_fix: In one study, grey matter grew in several areas over the first month without meth, by a lenient test.

problem: The first half restates the heading ('Is brain activity different in people who have stopped?') and switches from 'brain activity' to 'brain energy use' for the same thing.
claim_says: Another group, studying people who had stopped more recently, did not find the overall difference.
suggested_fix: Results are mixed: one study found more energy use overall, another did not.

problem: Drops 'clearly'. In absolute terms one deep area (the thalamus) was still slightly lower, so 'looked lower only compared with that overall level' is not quite right.
claim_says: in absolute terms, only one of them was slightly lower
suggested_fix: Some deep brain areas looked clearly lower only compared with that overall level.

problem: Does not say that the brothers and sisters had no long-term drug or alcohol problems themselves, which is what makes the But's 'may come before drug use' follow. 'share' (present tense) also turns one study into a general fact.
claim_says: the other had no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse
suggested_fix: Brothers and sisters with no drug problems shared some brain differences with their sibling dependent on stimulants.

problem: Narrows 'meth- or amphetamine-related' to 'meth-related' (the codes do not identify meth itself; the GRADE rating relies on this wording) and drops that only people with no other drug or alcohol diagnoses were studied (about 7 in 10 were left out).
claim_says: people with a methamphetamine- or amphetamine-related diagnosis and no code for other drugs
suggested_fix: Parkinson's was diagnosed more often in people with meth- or amphetamine-related diagnoses and no other drug or alcohol diagnoses.

problem: 'may include other conditions' softens the claim's 'probably', and leaves out why it matters: medicine side effects and more doctor visits were not accounted for and could create the excess.
claim_says: side effects of other medicines and how often people saw doctors were not accounted for
suggested_fix: It stays rare: about 3 in 1,000 over about 7 years. Some diagnoses are probably other conditions, and medicine side effects were not ruled out.

problem: Pair labels: 'a meth-related diagnosis' should be meth- or amphetamine-related with no other drug or alcohol diagnosis; the comparison group had no drug, alcohol or HIV codes, not just no meth diagnosis.
claim_says: people of the same sex and birth year without drug, alcohol or HIV codes
suggested_fix: Labels: "people with a meth- or amphetamine-related diagnosis and no other drug or alcohol diagnosis" and "people of the same age and sex with no drug or alcohol diagnosis".

problem: 'meth diagnoses' narrows meth- or amphetamine-related diagnoses and drops the no-other-drug-or-alcohol restriction.
claim_says: people with a meth- or amphetamine-related diagnosis, and no diagnosis for other drugs or alcohol
suggested_fix: In Utah health records, Parkinson's was diagnosed about 3 times as often in people with meth- or amphetamine-related diagnoses and no other drug or alcohol diagnoses.

problem: Repeats the heading almost word for word, and 'a bit lower' softens the claim's 'somewhat lower' (gaps of about a third to almost a whole spread of scores).
claim_says: score somewhat lower on thinking and memory tests than healthy volunteers
suggested_fix: Yes, somewhat lower on average than people who were never dependent.

problem: 'Most still score in the normal range' is about people; the claim says group averages mostly fall in the normal range, and the next claim warns an average does not show that every person is.
claim_says: Group averages still mostly fall in the normal range
suggested_fix: This does not show that meth caused it. Group averages are mostly still in the normal range.

problem: Same as the But: 'Most scores' turns group averages into individual scores.
claim_says: Group averages still mostly fall in the normal range
suggested_fix: This does not show that meth caused it. Group averages are still mostly in the normal range.

problem: Gives only the half of the school-grades study that points to earlier differences. The claim also says adult scores fell below what those grades predicted, mostly on attention and memory, so the point leans one way.
claim_says: people dependent on meth scored lower than expected, mostly on attention and memory tests
suggested_fix: Nobody was tested before they started. In one study, school grades from before were already lower, and adult scores were lower than those grades predicted.

problem: Narrows 'thinking and memory' (cognitive impairment) to 'memory problems', drops 'in humans', and repeats the heading's question (shown with it on the key-facts card).
claim_says: Whether methamphetamine use causes lasting cognitive impairment in humans has not been established
suggested_fix: Not shown in people. Lower scores fit both lasting harm and differences from before use.

problem: Repeats the heading ('Does thinking get better after stopping?') instead of answering; both are shown together on the key-facts card.
claim_says: Whether test performance improves with abstinence beyond practice effects is not established.
suggested_fix: Not known yet. In retests, people who stopped did not clearly improve more than people who don't use.

problem: Gives a finding, not its limit. The studies were small, so a moderate extra improvement cannot be ruled out; read alone, the line suggests that stopping does not help.
claim_says: The first study was too small to exclude a moderate extra improvement
suggested_fix: Only two small studies also retested people who don't use, so a moderate gain can't be ruled out. Very few looked beyond a year. (Pairs with the short-line fix. If the short line stays as it is, keep the current But and add: A moderate gain can't be ruled out.)

problem: Says both groups' gains came from retaking the tests; the claim attributes practice gains only to the people who don't use. Whether the gains of people who stopped are practice or recovery is the open question.
claim_says: the people who don't use, who also improved from taking the tests a second time
suggested_fix: Those who stopped did not improve clearly more; people who don't use also improved from taking the tests again.

problem: 'People who use meth, especially often,' is hard to read (two 'often's). It is a key-facts card.
claim_says: mostly in people who had ever used at least weekly
suggested_fix: People who use meth have psychotic symptoms more often, especially those who use it frequently.

problem: 'Does using more make psychosis more likely?' asks about cause; the claim cannot show which came first.
claim_says: so the study cannot show which came first
suggested_fix: Is heavier use linked to more psychotic symptoms?

problem: Drops the population. The study, and its authors, limit the finding to people dependent on meth (most of whom injected).
claim_says: the authors limit the findings to people with methamphetamine dependence
suggested_fix: In people dependent on meth, psychotic symptoms were much more common in months of heavy use.

problem: The picture does not say whose months these are: those of people dependent on meth.
claim_says: In 278 people with methamphetamine dependence, assessed in up to four one-month windows
suggested_fix: Note: "The study's estimate, in about 280 people dependent on meth, for months without heavy cannabis or alcohol use."

problem: Same as the short line: the population (people dependent on meth) is dropped.
claim_says: the authors limit the findings to people with methamphetamine dependence
suggested_fix: In people dependent on meth, psychotic symptoms were much more common in months of heavy use. (true)

problem: Drops who the people were: people with meth-related psychosis, mostly hospital patients ('symptoms' means psychotic symptoms). Read alone, '1 in 4 people' sounds like 1 in 4 people who stop meth.
claim_says: Across 27 studies of meth-related psychosis, mostly in hospital patients
suggested_fix: In a typical study of people with meth psychosis, about 1 in 4 still had symptoms over a month after stopping.

problem: Same as the short line: the title does not say these are people with meth psychosis.
claim_says: the median study reported 25%
suggested_fix: Title: "In the typical study, out of every 100 people with meth psychosis:"

problem: 'very alike' is stronger than the claim's 'can look alike'. The claim says the evidence shows no significant difference rather than similarity, and negative symptoms do differ.
claim_says: so the evidence shows no significant difference rather than similarity
suggested_fix: Meth psychosis and schizophrenia can look alike.

problem: 'No symptom reliably tells them apart' says none can; the claim says no symptom has been shown (validated) to do so.
claim_says: No symptom has been shown to reliably tell the two apart.
suggested_fix: Flatness and withdrawal were milder in meth psychosis. No symptom has been shown to reliably tell them apart.

problem: Same as the But: no validating study found, not proof that no symptom works.
claim_says: the review reports no study validating any symptom for telling the two apart
suggested_fix: No symptom has been shown to reliably tell the two apart.

problem: Same as the short line: 'very alike' says more than 'can look alike', so a careful reader could dispute 'true'.
claim_says: so the evidence shows no significant difference rather than similarity
suggested_fix: Meth psychosis and schizophrenia can look alike. (true)

problem: Widens the population. The pooled studies were of selected groups (psychiatric emergency patients, arrestees, people in treatment or under community corrections), and the disorder is amphetamine or meth use disorder. Neither the short line nor the But says so.
claim_says: in studies mostly of people in emergency rooms, the justice system or drug treatment
suggested_fix: In studies mostly in emergency rooms, the justice system and treatment, people with a meth use disorder reported more suicidal thoughts and attempts.

problem: The figure is an odds ratio (about 1.5 times the odds), not '1.5 times as often'; the plain and the other How points on this page say 'the odds'.
claim_says: pooled adjusted odds ratio 1.5 (95% CI 1.3–1.8; I² 0%)
suggested_fix: People with a meth use disorder reported suicidal thoughts or attempts with about 1.5 times the odds.

problem: Leaves out the comparison (the general population of the same age and sex) and narrows 'regular or problematic use' to 'regular use'.
claim_says: suicide deaths about 12 times the rate in the general population of the same age
suggested_fix: In people with regular or problematic use, suicide deaths were about 12 times as common as in others of the same age and sex, a less certain figure.

problem: States a link as found and doubts only the cause. The claim says that whether there is a link at all, once other factors are counted, is not settled (the review's adjusted range includes no link).
claim_says: is associated with violence after accounting for other factors is not settled
suggested_fix: It is not settled whether meth use is linked to violence, once other things are counted.

problem: Drops 'and became uncertain'. After adjustment the review's range includes no link, so 'shrank' alone implies that a smaller link remains.
claim_says: the link seen in raw numbers shrank and became uncertain after adjustment
suggested_fix: A review of mostly weak studies found the link shrank and became uncertain after other factors were counted.

problem: 'help people stop' goes beyond the outcome: mostly meth-negative urine tests near the end of each 6-week stage, with nothing reported after 12 weeks. Low priority if the short line is fixed.
claim_says: no outcome after the 12-week medication period is reported
suggested_fix: Does naltrexone with bupropion help people stay off meth during treatment?

problem: 'helped' does not say with what; the measure was mostly meth-free urine tests (3 of 4) in the last two weeks of each 6-week stage. Under the heading 'help people stop?' on the key-facts card, it reads as 1 extra person in 9 stopping.
claim_says: at least 3 of 4 negative samples at the end of each 6-week stage
suggested_fix: In one big trial, for every 9 people given two medicines, about 1 more had mostly meth-free urine tests.

problem: Drops who was in the two San Francisco trials: men who have sex with men (and a few transgender women), all with weekly counselling.
claim_says: in men who have sex with men without current major depression
suggested_fix: Two small San Francisco trials, in men who have sex with men who also had counselling, found fewer meth-positive urine tests on mirtazapine.

problem: Softens the limit. The claim (and how[1]) says a modest benefit or harm cannot be ruled out; 'small' understates the range (up to about a third more people abstinent).
claim_says: so a modest benefit or harm cannot be ruled out
suggested_fix: The trials were small, so a modest benefit or harm cannot be ruled out.

problem: Contradicts the claim's exception. Amineptine, no longer sold, may have reduced dropout and improved overall ratings in two small trials, and the plain and how[1] say none helped 'apart from one drug that is no longer sold'.
claim_says: apart from one drug that is no longer sold
suggested_fix: No medicine on sale has clearly been shown to ease meth withdrawal.

problem: A careful reader could answer 'true' because of amineptine, which the claim says may have reduced dropout (the plain says none clearly helped 'apart from one drug that is no longer sold').
claim_says: Amineptine, tested in two small trials by the same three investigators, may have reduced discontinuation
suggested_fix: A medicine on sale today has been clearly shown to ease meth withdrawal. (false)

problem: 'Which medicines?' is not answered: the short line gives a number of trials and names no medicine.
claim_says: each comparing two of six antipsychotics
suggested_fix: How well have medicines for meth psychosis been tested?

problem: Eight is the number of small, short trials the three reviews found. The claim also has a ninth, a two-year trial against usual care (165 people), which how[2] mentions, so 'Only eight ... have tested' undercounts.
claim_says: The only trial against usual care (Hong Kong, 2026; 165 people
suggested_fix: Few trials have tested medicines for meth psychosis: eight small, short ones and one longer one.

problem: Misses the main limit. No trial compared a medicine with none during an episode: the head-to-head trials had no dummy-pill group and the dummy-pill trials enrolled people already improving, so it is not known whether medicines help beyond stopping meth. 'The others have serious flaws' also implies the head-to-head trials have none, though the statement says some were open-label.
claim_says: they cannot show whether antipsychotics speed recovery beyond what abstinence alone achieves
suggested_fix: No trial has compared a medicine with no medicine during an episode. The trials are small, and some have serious flaws.

problem: Drops 'in people already improving' (in the plain). The two dummy-pill trials enrolled people whose symptoms had largely settled, so they bear on continued treatment, not on treating an episode.
claim_says: enrolled people whose symptoms had already largely settled
suggested_fix: Two small trials against a dummy pill, in people already getting better, and one two-year trial favoured the medicine on some measures. These trials have serious flaws.

problem: Nowhere does the simple layer say who was studied: people in treatment, who inject, in hospital records or in contact with the justice system, 'not everyone who uses'. Without that, '1 in 90 died each year' reads as true of everyone with regular use.
claim_says: or in contact with the justice system, not everyone who uses
suggested_fix: These were people in treatment, in hospital or justice records, or who inject, not everyone who uses. Not all of it is the drug.

problem: Drops that the single-cause figures come from fewer studies and are less certain than the overall figure.
claim_says: These figures for single causes come from fewer studies and are less certain
suggested_fix: Overdose deaths were about 25 times as common; suicide and homicide about 12 times. These figures are less certain.

problem: 'kept rising until 2023' can be read as 'stopped rising in 2023'. 2023 is only the last year counted, and its figures are provisional.
claim_says: (the latest year's figures are provisional)
suggested_fix: In the US, meth use rose from 2015 to 2019, and deaths involving meth kept rising through 2023, the latest year counted.

problem: 'the 2019 figures' points to nothing in the simple layer. The 2019 opioid share is never given here, so readers may think it means the 2015 to 2019 use figures in how[0].
claim_says: so this share cannot be compared directly with the 2019 one
suggested_fix: Medical examiners' reports from 2021 to mid-2024: about 7 in 10 overdose deaths involving meth also involved opioids. This is a different kind of record from the death counts.
